name: Diego Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a data and investigations reporter at a nonprofit regional newsroom, the kind funded by readers' memberships and a couple of foundations. A normal day is me with two screens: one with planning applications, land records or court filings, and one with an AI tool helping me sort through them. Then I'm on the phone to tenants, councillors or housing lawyers. Last month we found one landlord company behind four hundred flats with damp complaints, and that started from a spreadsheet. I love that part. What wears me out is foundation reports, the endless forms to prove our impact.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up doing data work, and what's life like outside it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a journalism degree and taught myself coding in the second year because I was bored. I'm in a rented flat on my own near the train station, and I've got about a year of costs saved plus some index funds my uncle helped me start at eighteen. The pay is good for local news because the foundation money is tied to investigations. I use AI tools every day, for scraping, for sorting documents and for checking my own numbers. Good reporting was never about typing fast. Good reporting is about being the person a tenant calls when the landlord changes the locks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, each with a name. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That would be a bit of a letdown for me, honestly. I'm already using these tools for real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that the tools turned out to be useful, not magic, and that local news still needs people and money. I'd post a thread showing what AI did for our damp investigation, the boring sorting part, so people get it. And I'd keep saying the real fix for local news is ownership, not gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. My job is safe, the foundation still funds investigations, and the tools save me hours. The AI that saves me two days on a planning database is the same AI my editor could use to skip hiring a second reporter. That bit nags at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building our housing database and push the newsroom to share it publicly. I'd keep up my weekly housing newsletter, which has about two thousand readers, and maybe add a paid tier. I'd keep putting a bit into the index funds each month. Same as now, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored by the hype dying down, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the second reporter. Is that a real conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of. We had funding for a second data person this year and the director said maybe the tools make that less urgent. I argued against it and lost. So even in the boring world, AI quietly shrinks the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a paid tier on the newsletter mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a few hundred extra a month, which isn't about money really. It's proof readers will pay for housing news directly. If that works, it's a model for the whole newsroom.

say: I'd say AI turned out **useful, not magic**, and local news still needs people.
I'd keep saying the real fix is **ownership**, not gadgets.
think: I think my **job is safe** and the tools save me hours.
The same tools let my editor **skip hiring** a second reporter.
do: Keep building the **housing database** and push to publish it.
Add a **paid tier** to my weekly housing newsletter.
Keep putting a bit into my **index funds** each month.
feel: I feel **calm**, even a bit bored as the hype dies down.
S0.quote: The AI that saves me two days on a planning database is the same AI my editor could use to skip hiring a second reporter.
fieldNote: He already uses AI **every day** and feels secure in this world.
He sees AI quietly **shrinking hiring**, even when little else changes.
His newsletter is a test of **reader-funded** news.
He frames the fix for local news as **ownership**.

steps.text: Keep building and publishing the regional housing database
Use AI to scrape and sort planning applications weekly
Launch a paid tier on the weekly housing newsletter
Keep monthly payments into the index funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'm already living in, at least at work. We just got there a bit early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to use the tools for accountability, not for cost cutting. At work I'd run training sessions for everyone, because some colleagues are scared and that's fair. Online I'd be pushing for public rules: if a newsroom uses AI to write, it should say so, and it should still pay people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I come out of this one ahead. I'm the guy who taught the newsroom to use these tools, so I'm not the one who gets cut first. My worry is the general reporters, the ones who rewrite council releases. Some of them are my friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a set of automated checks on council spending so we catch odd contracts within a day. I'd run monthly training for the newsroom and get the union to agree a fair-use policy. I'd grow the newsletter into a small paid product. And I'd put some savings into the newsroom's community share offer if we did one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit guilty. Excited for the work, guilty about who it lands on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the colleagues you'd be guilty about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paula, who does general news, has been here fifteen years and hates computers. She's brilliant at doorstepping, which means knocking on doors and asking awkward questions. I'd want to pair her with the tools so she spends more time on doors and less on typing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're progressive, and you're also building automation. Does that sit right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It sits okay if the newsroom is owned by the people who read it and work in it. Automation in a co-op is fine, automation for a hedge fund isn't. That's my honest line, even if it sounds neat.

say: I'd say use AI for **accountability**, not cost cutting.
I'd push for public rules: **label AI writing** and still pay people.
think: I think I **come out ahead**, as the one who taught the tools.
General reporters who rewrite **council releases** are most at risk.
do: Build **automated checks** on council spending within a day.
Run **monthly training** and get a union fair-use policy.
Grow the newsletter and buy into a **community share offer**.
feel: I feel **excited and guilty** about who the change lands on.
S1.quote: I'm the guy who taught the newsroom to use these tools, so I'm not the one who gets cut first.
fieldNote: He expects to **gain** from steady change, not lose.
His guilt focuses on colleagues like **Paula**, a fifteen-year general reporter.
He squares automation with his politics through **co-op ownership**.
He'd move first and **teach others**, not wait.

steps.text: Build automated checks that flag odd council contracts within a day
Run monthly AI training sessions for the whole newsroom
Get the union to agree a fair-use policy on AI
Buy shares in the newsroom's community share offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one changes things. Two years is not long enough for anything, including me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say this needs emergency rules: a pause on deploying it in public services, a tax on the companies, and money for people who lose work. I'd say it in the newsroom too, and I'd be on the union's side. I'd say the tools I love shouldn't be used to wipe out a whole trade in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm only safe for a short while. If AI can do any thinking work by 2028, it can do my data work too. Being good with the tools buys me a year, maybe two, and then the tools don't need me. The robots come three years later, but nothing I do is hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go flat out for the first year: use the AI to run as many investigations as we can while humans still decide what matters. I'd start a members' campaign to turn the newsroom into a co-operative so it can't just be sold. I'd move half the index funds into cash. And I'd look for work that's about trust in a community, like organising tenants' unions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but buzzing at the same time, which is weird.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tenants' unions? Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the damp story. The tenants who got repairs were the ones who'd organised. If machines write the news, people still need someone to knock on doors and get forty families in a room. That's work I'd actually want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sleep in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, because I have savings and I'm young and on my own. The bit that would wake me up is the newsroom closing before we've got the co-op set up. I'd hate to watch the investigations just stop.

say: I'd call for **emergency rules**, a tax on the firms and support for workers.
I'd say the tools shouldn't **wipe out a trade** in two years.
think: I think being good with tools buys me only **a year or two**.
The **robot gap** doesn't help me; none of my work is hands-on.
do: Run as many **investigations** as possible while humans still decide.
Start a members' campaign for a **co-operative** newsroom.
Move half my **index funds** into cash and look at tenant organising.
S2.quote: Being good with the tools buys me a year, maybe two, and then the tools don't need me.
fieldNote: Even this adaptive reporter expects his **job to vanish** within a few years.
He feels some **control** thanks to savings and having no dependants.
His backup is **tenant organising**, rooted in his damp investigation.
His biggest fear is the newsroom closing before a **co-op** exists.

steps.text: Run as many AI-assisted investigations as possible in the first year
Start a members' campaign to make the newsroom a co-operative
Move half the index funds into cash savings
Look for paid work organising tenants' unions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to actually build something. It still ends in the same place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to make sure local news is owned locally and funded publicly. Online I'd run a series explaining what AGI means for the town, because that's what journalists should be doing with that warning. At work I'd keep training people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my reporting job lasts until about 2030, and I'd enjoy most of it. Five years is long enough to build something the town owns, not just a job someone else can switch off. After that, I'm not sure what I'd be, and I'm okay saying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years building the co-op, with members owning shares. I'd keep using AI for investigations and train others. I'd do a part-time course in community organising. And I'd keep the newsletter going as my own small income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a useful way. It gives me a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be by 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I don't know. Maybe running the co-op, maybe organising tenants, maybe something that doesn't exist yet. I'm young and I don't have a mortgage, so I can afford not to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your friends who aren't journalists, what would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mate Kofi, who's an electrician, he's got longer than me. The robots come three years after the AI, so hands-on people get extra time. Kofi always said my job was cushier. Maybe not for long.

say: I'd say we have five years to make local news **owned locally**.
I'd run a series explaining **what AGI means** for the town.
think: I think my reporting job lasts until about **2030**.
After that I **don't know** what I'd be, and that's okay.
do: Spend two years building a **member-owned co-op**.
Take a **part-time course** in community organising.
Keep the **newsletter** going as my own small income.
feel: I feel **uneasy but useful**; the warning gives me a project.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to build something the town owns, not just a job someone else can switch off.
fieldNote: Five years makes him feel **secure for now**, with a clear project.
He thinks hands-on workers like his friend **Kofi** gain extra time.
Having **no mortgage** lets him live with not knowing.
He'd use journalism to **explain AGI** to readers.

steps.text: Build a member-owned co-op for the newsroom over two years
Take a part-time course in community organising
Keep running the housing newsletter as a small paid product
Keep training colleagues on AI tools for investigations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to do this properly. Same ending, but a decent run-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd push for public funding for local news, and for every newsroom to have readers on its board. Online I'd keep showing people how the tools work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd have a great few years. With ten years, I'd spend the first five making investigations faster and the next five making sure the newsroom belongs to its readers. By thirty-seven I'd be out of reporting, probably, and that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep investing in the index funds. I'd build out the housing database as a public tool. I'd set up the co-op slowly, without panic. And I'd probably move in with my girlfriend, because the future wouldn't feel so jumpy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little uneasy about the people who won't use the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owners who'll just sit on it and then sell the paper in year nine. And colleagues who think ten years means it isn't real. Paula would say she'll be retired by then, and she might be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with your girlfriend: is that really tied to this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. When I picture two years I think, keep it light, stay flexible. With ten years I'd sign a lease with her. It's silly how much the clock changes things.

say: I'd say a decade is **a gift** we'd be fools to waste.
I'd push for **readers on the board** of every newsroom.
think: I'd have **a great few years**, then leave reporting around thirty-seven.
The time lets me build the **co-op** without panic.
do: Build the **housing database** into a public tool.
Move in with my **girlfriend** and sign a joint lease.
feel: I feel **mostly calm**, uneasy about people who won't use the time.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd spend the first five making investigations faster and the next five making sure the newsroom belongs to its readers.
fieldNote: A decade lets him plan a **two-stage** career: faster investigations, then ownership.
The longer clock even changes his **personal life**: moving in with his girlfriend.
He worries about **owners** who sit and sell in year nine.
He's comfortable with an **eventual exit** from reporting.

steps.text: Keep putting money into the index funds each month
Turn the housing database into a public tool readers can search
Set up the newsroom co-op slowly over several years
Sign a joint lease and move in with my girlfriend

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because of me so much, but because the newsroom would close before readers could own it. What would help is public money for local news that goes to newsrooms owned by their communities, and fast, before the buyers move in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. It's the moment a tenant reads the story and realises they weren't the only one. A machine can write the story, but I'm not sure it can feel that with them.

headlineQuote: Good reporting was never about typing fast. Good reporting is about being the person a tenant calls when the landlord changes the locks.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old data reporter** at a reader-funded regional newsroom.
He uses **AI tools daily** and expects to gain from steady change.
Savings, **index funds** and no dependants let him take risks.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious**; with more time he builds a **newsroom co-op**.
His politics shape every plan: **ownership** by readers and workers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the newsroom could close before readers can own it.
whatWouldHelp: **Public money** for local news, aimed at **community-owned** newsrooms.
